                                 I.      INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY

          Oncor Electric Delivery Company, LLC (Oncor) and LCRA Transmission Services

Corporation (LCRA TSC) (collectively, the Applicants) seek to amend their certificates of

convenience and necessity (CCN) for the proposed Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation

765-kV transmission line project in Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano, Mason,

McCulloch, Menard, Milam, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and Williamson counties.

The Applicants propose to construct, own, and operate a new single-circuit 765-kV transmission

line between Oncor’s existing Bell County Switch and LCRA TSC’s existing Big Hill Substation.

          As an initial matter, the Staff (Staff) of the Public Utility Commission of Texas

(Commission) reiterates that the Applicants complied with the notice requirements and that

Proposed Project is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the

public. 1

                                    V.      PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES

     A. Preliminary Order Issue No. 1: Adequacy of Application and Number of Routes

          Staff addressed this issue in its initial brief.

     B. Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 2–3: Notice of Application and Notice of Public Meeting

          Staff maintains that the Applicants provided proper notice of the application in compliance

with PURA § 37.054 and 16 TAC § 22.52(a). 7 Many intervenors raise concerns about the

Applicants’ notice in their initial briefs. 8 In summary, many of the intervenors’ concerns take issue

with receiving notice of the application in late March 2026 once the application was filed, but they

did not receive notice of any of the Applicants’ June 2025 public meetings. 9 The intervenors argue

the parties who received notice of the public meetings had more time to prepare than the parties

who only received notice of the application. 10

          For example, Kevin Kennedy argues the Applicants failed to provide proper notice,

because the Applicants mailed notice of the application to more parties than the number of parties

noticed of the Applicants’ June 2025 Public Meetings. 11 Mr. Kennedy argues the affected

landowners who were not given notice of the public meetings were denied the opportunity to

“participate or prepare during the preliminary phase.” 12 However, these notice concerns and

arguments confuse the notice requirement under 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3) and the notice of public

meeting requirement under 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4) as being one and the same.

           Instead, these two requirements are separate and distinct. Under 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4), the

Applicants were required to hold “at least one public meeting prior to the filing of its licensing

application if 25 or more persons would be entitled to receive direct mail of the notice of the

application.” Under 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3), the Applicants were required to mail notice of its

application to affected landowners on the date they filed their application. Further, under 16 TAC

§ 22.52(a)(3)(F), the Applicants were required to file a supplemental affidavit of notice to cure any

insufficient notices. The Applicants complied with such requirements.

          Therefore, by treating these two separate requirements as one, the intervenors seek to

expand what is currently required under 16 TAC § 22.52(a). Under the intervenors’ interpretation,

the Applicants would be required to continuously hold public meetings until the Applicants file

their application. But that is not what the rules require. Accordingly, because the Applicants

complied with the notice requirements under PURA § 37.054 and 16 TAC § 22.52(a), Staff

maintains that the Applicants provided proper notice of the application.

     C. Preliminary Order Issue No. 4: Public Input

     D. Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 5–7: Need

          Staff reiterates its position that the proposed project is necessary for the service,

accommodation, convenience, and safety of the public. 13 The Proposed Project constitutes Import

Path 2, which the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), an independent organization

under PURA § 39.151, has determined is needed for system reliability. And such determination is

entitled to great weight from the Commission pursuant to 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II).

           As discussed in Staff’s Initial Brief, H.B 5066 ordered the Commission to “develop a plan”

to implement the PBRP to ensure the development and approval of necessary transmission

improvements to the area. 14 ERCOT worked with transmission and distribution service providers,

as well as received input from stakeholder at monthly meetings, in its development of the PBRP. 15

Using load forecasting requirements established in H.B. 5066, ERCOT confirmed that new

transmission facilities are needed to support the reliability and adequacy of the transmission

system. 16 Contrary to several claims that the new transmission facilities are needed due to

unsubstantiated artificial intelligence and data center projects, ERCOT specified that these new

facilities are required due to the continued unprecedented load growth in the Permian Basin by oil

and gas development. 17 ERCOT further concluded that a 765-kV “backbone [is] needed to increase

import capability into the Permian Basin and [to] support reliable service.” 18

          Furthermore, the needs of the specific geographic area surrounding the Proposed Project

are not determinative. Instead, the Commission “should consider the needs of the interconnected

statewide transmission system.” 19 More specifically, when determining whether to grant or amend

a CCN and particularly whether there will be a probable improvement of service or lowering of

cost to consumers in the area, the determination is not limited to the particular location of the

transmission lines. 20

           The Proposed Project will traverse 14 counties 21 over a span of over 200 miles 22 in order

to address the significant reliability issues of the Permian Basin, as acknowledged by the Texas

State Legislature, the Commission and ERCOT. The stated purpose of the Proposed Project does

not, and is not required to, address the need of the counties it will cross through. Rather, the

Proposed Project’s purpose is to “increase the reliability and resilience of the system, [and] support

import capability into the Permian Basin Region.” 23 Staff thus maintains that the Proposed Project

is needed for overall system stability and transmission reliability in the Permian Basin Region.

          Staff also reiterates its position that the Proposed Project is the best option when compared

to other non-transmission-related alternatives that some intervenors argue should be considered. 24

The Proposed Project, as mentioned above, is intended to address transmission reliability and

import issues that were identified by ERCOT. Compared to the alternatives, ERCOT identified

numerous customer benefits born by the 765-kV plan, such as nearly a billion dollars less in

construction-related outage costs and over $200 million in annual consumer energy cost savings. 25

Additionally, the Commission approved 765-kV import paths and tasked Applicants with the

construction of Import Path 2, which is the intended goal of the Proposed Project. 26 Ultimately,

generation alternatives cannot provide the necessary import capacities and transmission-related

shortcomings. 27

           In sum, Staff concludes that the Proposed Project is necessary to ensure the reliability,

resilience, and adequacy of the ERCOT transmission system in response to the unprecedented

growth continuing to take place in the Permian Basin region. Because the project benefits the

reliability issues of the statewide grid and is the most effective transmission solution identified by

ERCOT and approved by the Commission, Staff maintains that the Proposed Project satisfies the

statutory requirements of need under PURA and Commission rules.

     E. Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 8–10: Routing

          Based on Staff’s analysis of the routing criteria under PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC

§ 25.101(b)(3)(B), as discussed in Staff’s initial brief, 28 Staff reiterates its recommendation that

the Commission select Route 487. Although no proposed routes can entirely avoid negative

impacts, Route 487 reflects a reasonable and balanced approach that moderates impacts on the

affected communities and landowners while meeting statutory requirements. In terms of the initial

briefs filed by intervenors, many arguments raised to contest the viability of Route 487 have

already been discussed and rebutted by other intervenors. However, for purposes of best informing

the decision for the proposal decision, Staff respectfully replies regarding the following issues.

Methodology

          In response to 4K Land and Cattle Company’s (4K Land) argument that a documented and

reproduceable methodology is needed for determining the best route, 29 it is Staff’s position that

PURA § 37.056 and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) do not require a documented methodology nor

prescribe a quantifiable weight for each particular factor. Accordingly, 4K Land’s argument that

Staff’s witness, John Poole, and the Applicants did not use a documented methodology that can be

 “validated and verifiable” as conducted and advocated by its expert, James E. Scott, III, should be

          First, Staff reiterates, and 4K Land acknowledges, that PURA and Commission Rules

govern this proceeding. 31 Under PURA § 37.056(a), the Commission may grant a CCN only if it

finds that it is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.

PURA § 37.056(c) provides the routing criteria to be considered in an electric CCN proceeding,

including community values, parks, and recreational areas, historical values, aesthetic values, and

environmental integrity. Further, 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) provides additional criteria to be

considered in an electric CCN, such as engineering constraints, cost, moderation of impact on

affected community and landowners, use of compatible rights-of-way, paralleling existing rights-

of-way, and prudent avoidance. As required by PURA and Commission Rules, Mr. Poole weighed

the factors above and recommends Route 487. 32 Nothing in PURA or Commission Rules requires

a documented methodology or prescribes a quantifiable weight for a particular factor. 33

          Separate from 4K Land’s attempts to discredit Mr. Poole and Staff’s recommendation on

Route 487, Staff otherwise notes that several intervenors oppose Route 487 on the basis that it

does not perform well in terms of community values, recreational park areas and aesthetic values,

and environmental integrity, and therefore should not be selected as the route for this Proposed

Project. Staff further notes that several intervenors attempt to undervalue the extent to which Route

487 performs well in terms of costs and use of existing corridors (including apparent property

boundaries).

          Community Values

          To consider community values, the Commission should be cognizant of the issues

prioritized by the community during the public meeting process and avoid overvaluing and tallying

up the priorities of the intervenors who have filed testimony and participated in the hearing and

briefing process. While the evaluation of specific routing criteria may benefit from individual

landowner on-the-ground representations, each individual landowner ultimately prioritizes their

land over others, such that many intervenors have overtly followed the NIMBY-line of argument.

          Regarding the latter, some intervenors argue that the number of intervenors that oppose a

specific segment or route should be a governing factor. 42 However, as noted by other intervenors,

because all properties will be negatively affected to some degree or another, it is important to not

let the routing choice be determined based on a popularity contest in terms of the number of parties

supporting or opposing particular routes. 43 Notably, each route has its fair share of opposition. 44

prioritized by the community during the public meeting process and avoid overvaluing and tallying

briefing process. While the evaluation of specific routing criteria may benefit from individual

landowner on-the-ground representations, each individual landowner ultimately prioritizes their

land over others, such that many intervenors have overtly followed the NIMBY-line of argument.
